name: Bear's grease hair pomade

card.summary: Bear's grease was a rendered-fat pomade used for centuries to dress hair, add shine and, in marketing claims, promote hair growth.
card.note: Historical product; many commercial versions were actually pig fat.

quick.overview:
Bear's grease is rendered bear fat used as a scented pomade for hair. In Europe it was sold as a remedy for baldness and a styling dressing; Native American groups used it to make hair shine.

The appearance payoff was glossy, styled hair, and claimed regrowth. Historical claims were not tested in modern trials.
quick.how: The fat was washed, melted and strained, then scented; later commercial pots were sold in chemist shops. Users applied it to hair daily.
quick.risks: No modern safety data. Historic products were often adulterated with pork fat or lard.

lead: Bear's grease is the rendered fat of bears, used as a hair pomade in Europe and by many Native American groups. It was long marketed as a baldness remedy on the idea that bears' thick coats would transfer to people.[1]

Writers including Dioscorides in the first century and Nicholas Culpeper in 1653 recommended it for hair loss.[1] Atkinsons of London became the best-known seller, with a chained-bear logo, and kept it in production until after World War I.[1] As demand outstripped supply, makers substituted pig fat, suet and lard, scented with lavender, thyme or rose; one 1850s estimate held that about 99 percent of English "bear grease" contained pig fat.[1]
Among the Sauk, Huron and Delaware, men and women applied bear grease daily to make hair shinier.[1]

angle.text: Users applied it for shine and hold; marketers claimed it regrew hair. Gloss was the plainly visible effect.

infobox: Antiquity to about World War I

paras: Bear fat was a popular remedy for male hair loss from at least about 70 CE until about World War I.[1] Dioscorides described rendering the fat by washing, melting and straining.[1] Grokipedia adds that a London apothecary named Townsend is credited with an early 17th-century product, though this account is less certain.[2]
George Cruikshank's 1823 cartoon alludes to Russian bear grease, then considered the best.[1]

timeline.event: Culpeper writes that bear fat stops hair falling out.[1]
Cruikshank cartoon references Russian bear grease.[1]
